articleHeadline: 什么是血吸虫病？如何防范？中疾控解答
articleSummary: Schistosomiasis (schistosome disease), mainly caused by Schistosoma japonicum in China, is a waterborne zoonosis distributed across Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Transmission requires the snail Oncomelania hupensis as the intermediate host. In the lifecycle, eggs excreted in feces hatch into miracidia in water, infect snails to produce cercariae, which penetrate human or animal skin and become schistosomula that migrate to the liver and venous systems to mature and lay eggs, triggering inflammation where eggs deposit (intestines, liver). Clinically, acute infection features fever, diarrhea (mucous/pus), hepatosplenomegaly and cough; chronic infection varies, and late disease can cause severe wasting, ascites, splenomegaly, and portal hypertension. In China, April–October is the peak season due to rainfall and snail proliferation. Prevention emphasizes avoiding contact with contaminated water, using protective gear when unavoidable, safe boiled water, fecal waste management, livestock management, and early diagnosis and treatment.

articleHeadline: 麻疹、水痘、手足口病，什么时候最容易传染？
articleSummary: As of 2026-04-09, the article notes that contagiousness in fever-with-rash illnesses peaks around rash onset, not during fever. It classifies rash-onset patterns: fever before rash (e.g., infantile exanthema); simultaneous fever and rash (varicella, rubella, hand-foot-mouth disease); and rash after fever (measles) with the highest transmission risk. Infection begins in the respiratory or digestive tract, followed by viremia and dissemination; the rash reflects immune clearance. Transmission is highest during rash due to peak shedding in respiratory secretions and vesicular fluids, coughing/sneezing, and misperception of recovery. Common diseases: measles—airborne/droplet; infectious roughly 5 days before to 5 days after rash. Chickenpox—airborne and direct contact; contagious from 1–2 days before rash until all lesions crust. HFMD—droplets, contact, fecal-oral; higher risk about one week after rash. Prevention: isolation on diagnosis, hand hygiene and disinfection, stay-at-home when ill, vaccination (MMR, varicella, EV-A71 for HFMD). Source: Shanghai Hotline.

articleSummary: Three equine encephalitis viruses—Venezuelan (VEEV), Eastern (EEEV), and Western (WEEV)—could be simultaneously neutralized by a synthetic 'Trojan' protein developed by American molecular biologists at the University of Washington. The approach embeds core elements of the three viral receptors into a single peptide that binds all three viruses and effectively tricks them into attempting entry, thereby neutralizing infection. The concept, validated in mouse experiments, showed protection of 75% to 100% of treated animals, while all members of the untreated control group died by days 7–8. Historically, these viruses cause equine and human encephalitis; WEEV outbreaks were recently reported in Uruguay. There was no universal treatment prior to this work. The team conducted computer modeling to design several variants, selected the most effective, and confirmed promising results in vivo, indicating strong potential for a therapeutic against equine encephalitis outbreaks in horses and potentially humans.

articleSummary: As of 2026-04-09, cholera is an infection of the small intestine caused by Vibrio cholerae. The bacterium’s enterotoxin triggers sudden, profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting. El Tor biotype tends to cause milder disease than the classic biotype. More than 90% of infections are mild or moderate; less than 10% develop typical cholera with dehydration that can be life-threatening. Mortality without treatment ranges from 25% to 50%. Cholera is endemic in India and Southeast Asia, with outbreaks that can occur sporadically anywhere where water, sanitation, and hygiene practices are inadequate. Transmission is most often via food and water contaminated with Vibrio cholerae. Diagnosis relies on patient history and stool examination. Main treatment is fluid and electrolyte replacement; in severe cases, antibiotics can reduce the volume and duration of diarrhea and the period of bacterial excretion.

articleSummary: CMNV, a virus previously confined to shrimp and fish, is linked to chronic intraocular disease in humans as persistent ocular hypertension and viral uveitis (POH-VAU) in China. Electron microscopy found ~25-nm viral particles in ocular tissues; genetic analysis showed 98.96% identity to the aquatic-animal version. This is the first evidence that a marine-origin virus can trigger a specific ophthalmic disease in humans, prompting a reevaluation of seafood handling safety standards.

articleSummary: Prosthetic joint infection (PJI) is driving rising failure rates after total hip and knee arthroplasty globally as of 2026-04-09. Infections occur in approximately 0.5-1% of primary hip and knee replacements, with risk up to fourfold higher in revision surgeries. Cumulative infection incidence over time is about 1-1.5%, higher in knee than hip, and early postoperative infections within the first three months show an upward trend in some registries. Obesity nearly doubles the risk of infection-related revision in hip replacements, and older, medically complex patients are increasingly undergoing these procedures, contributing to the burden. Late infections occurring years after surgery are increasingly recognized. Management of PJI is costly and often requires two-stage revision with implant removal, prolonged antibiotics, and delayed reimplantation; costs can be four to five times higher than primary replacement. Preventive strategies include risk-factor optimization, perioperative protocols, improved implants, and early diagnosis to reduce need for extensive revisions.

articleSummary: Lumajang, East Java, Indonesia reports 105 suspected measles cases in babies and children for 2026 up to week 14. Blood samples from these cases are being tested at the Public Health Laboratory Center of the Ministry of Health in Surabaya, with results pending due to high volume. Although still classified as suspected, patients are treated as measles cases to prevent spread. Health workers will conduct home visits to identify additional cases, provide treatment, and implement limited isolation where needed. If household contacts show signs of infection, they will receive treatment and temporary isolation. Vaccination around the affected area will be offered to children not fully immunized, including catch-up immunizations if immunization is incomplete or overdue. Indonesia’s routine measles vaccination starts at 9 months, with boosters at 18–24 months and again in first grade to maintain immunity.

articleHeadline: Five Children Die Of Suspected Encephalitis In Rajasthan, Health Dept On Alert
articleSummary: Five children aged 1–4 died in Salumbar district, Rajasthan, in recent days amid a suspected viral encephalitis outbreak. articleHeadline: China issues measures to prevent dengue fever import amid global surge
articleSummary: China's General Administration of Customs issues dengue fever import prevention measures, effective 2026-04-10 for one year. articleSummary: Pertussis (whooping cough) in China poses a severe risk to infants and young children. articleHeadlineTranslated: A virus from seafood has jumped to humans and causes a chronic disease
articleHeadline: Un virus din fructele de mare a trecut la oameni și provoacă o boală cronică
articleSummary: China reports rising cases of viral anterior uveitis with persistent ocular hypertension (POH-VAU). In a study of 70 patients diagnosed between January 2022 and April 2025, researchers found ~25-nm viral particles in ocular tissues by electron microscopy, absent in controls. Gold-labeled antibodies specific to CMNV and genome sequencing showing 98.96% identity with CMNV variants from aquatic animals link CMNV to this human ocular disease. Nearly 75% of patients reported handling raw seafood or consuming raw aquatic products. Cell culture and mice experiments showed infected animals developed symptoms including raised intraocular pressure, supporting causation. This is the first human-eye disease associated with an aquatic animal virus. CMNV has been detected in 49 species (crabs, mollusks) across Asia, Africa, Europe, Antarctica, and the Americas. Published in Nature Microbiology.

articleSummary: Covert Mortality Nodavirus (CMNV), previously detected in shrimp and other marine life, is under investigation for a possible human eye disease. articleSummary: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a contagious viral illness that primarily affects young children, spreading rapidly in preschools. The virus has about a 2-day incubation, with symptoms appearing around day 3. Early signs include fever, sore throat, malaise, and reduced appetite; children may be irritable and tired. In the classic phase, see skin and mucosal lesions: red spots or blisters on the hands, feet, inside the mouth or on the tongue; eating difficulties. Some may have mild diarrhea. Most cases are mild and self-limiting, but warning signs require urgent care: persistent crying or inconsolable sleep, high fever, tremors, breathing difficulties, unsteady gait. Transmission is via fecal-oral routes and direct contact; prevention centers on hygiene: handwashing, avoiding crowds during outbreaks, masking when outdoors, cleaning toys. Hue health authorities report rising HFMD cases versus the same period and stress early detection and hygiene.

articleSummary: In Zhengzhou, Henan Province, a 35-year-old pregnant woman died after Listeria monocytogenes infection traced to leftovers stored in her refrigerator. Despite three months of intensive treatment, she passed away just two days after her 35th birthday. Listeria is particularly dangerous for pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals and can cause miscarriage or neonatal death. The bacteria survive at freezing temperatures (even at -20°C for up to a year) and are common in meat and dairy products. After infection, symptoms often include diarrhea; vulnerable people may develop meningitis or sepsis. Long incubation ranges from about 1–3 weeks, sometimes 2 months, complicating source identification. Foods at risk include unpasteurized dairy, ready-to-eat meats, salads, sandwiches, and pre-cut fruits; cantaloupe/stone fruits can harbor contamination on rinds. Prevention emphasizes fridge temperature at ≤4°C, avoid overcrowding, separate raw and cooked foods, heat leftovers for ≥10 minutes, and seek care for fever or diarrhea.

articleSummary: Leptospirosis, caused by Leptospira sp., poses a serious threat to dogs in Indonesia, particularly during the rainy season when damp environments and standing water facilitate transmission from infected rats. Direct exposure occurs via contact with infected urine; indirect exposure via contaminated water or soil also spreads infection. Early, non-specific signs in dogs include fever, shivering, muscle pain, lethargy, decreased appetite, and increased thirst with dehydration, along with diarrhea or vomiting. Severe cases may progress to jaundice of the skin, gums, and whites of the eyes, indicating kidney and liver injury and risk of death if untreated. Vaccination is the most effective preventive measure, with annual boosters maintaining protective antibody levels and aiding recovery if infection occurs. Additional precautions include avoiding polluted standing water during walks, washing the dog's coat and feet after outdoor activities, and maintaining a rodent-controlled home environment. As of 9 April 2026, awareness is crucial.

articleHeadline: Fecal metatranscriptomics and virus isolation reveal picornavirus diversity and evolution in Japanese wild boars and pigs - Scientific Reports
articleSummary: Japan-wide fecal metatranscriptomics and virus isolation from 300 wild boars and 363 domestic pigs (2017–2023) reveal extensive picornavirus (PVs) diversity in wild boar and pig enteric viromes. ST-cell inoculation yielded cytopathic effects in 47 wild boars and 178 pigs. Sequencing yielded 42 wild-type PVs and 247 tissue culture–adapted PVs. Among 67 porcine teschovirus (PTV) strains, 66 were isolated (3 wild boars, 63 pigs) across 11 serotypes with intertypic recombination; one wild boar PTV resembled Japanese porcine strains, while another diverged, suggesting independent evolution. EV-G strains (73) spanned nine genotypes; G17 and G6 predominated in both hosts. PL-CP sequences were detected in six EV-G genotypes, with tc-type PL-CP–positive G2, G8, and G18 reported for the first time. PSV strains totaled 126 (14 wild boars, 112 pigs) and showed region-specific clustering and recombination; PKV was detected in wild boars in Japan for the first time. SaV GIII was most frequent; a wild boar GXI strain clustered with GXI but had low VP1 similarity, and its 3′ end matched Chinese GVII.5, suggesting cross-species transmission. PVs diversify via recombination in wild boar and pig populations.

articleSummary: Five-month-old stray kitten in Mumbai, Maharashtra, died within a day after severe breathing problems, revealing a first-known domestic feline infection with Mycobacterium orygis, a TB-related bacterium already seen in humans, cattle, and wildlife in South Asia. articleSummary: Guatemala confirms its first chikungunya case in Catarina, San Marcos, ending a decade without local transmission. The infection is linked to the Mexico border region, where 12 cases have been reported in Chiapas and Quintana Roo; four suspected cases are reported in Escuintla, Chiquimula and Guatemala. articleSummary: Cholera evolves through an arms race between Vibrio cholerae and bacteriophages. Higher ICP1 lytic phage load in patients correlates with milder disease, while loss of anti-phage systems links to severe disease and greater spread beyond Bangladesh. India and Bangladesh have experienced 20+ years of separate V. cholerae evolution, constrained by borders. Lysogenic phage K139, infecting V. cholerae O1, carries glo gene associated with virulence in mouse models, informing pandemics from its global source.

articleHeadline: Silent invaders: Mosquitoes and sandflies spreading in new areas
articleSummary: Kenya’s arid northern counties report emergence of new vectors driving visceral leishmaniasis and malaria. Since 2023, visceral leishmaniasis cases have expanded beyond endemic areas to Tharaka Nithi and Kajiado; Marsabit and Turkana counties show rising cases across new villages, with both visceral and cutaneous leishmaniasis now present in Kajiado. The study identifies Anopheles stephensi, an invasive malaria vector from South Asia/Middle East, in Kenya after detections in Djibouti, Ethiopia, Sudan, Somalia, Nigeria and Ghana; this urban-adapted mosquito breeds in man-made containers and may heighten urban malaria risk. Leishmaniasis vectors now include Phlebotomus orientalis expanding into Marsabit, Turkana, Mandera (previously Sudan/Ethiopia/Sinai Egypt), and Phlebotomus alexandri detected in Isiolo and spreading to Marsabit, Turkana, Wajir, Kajiado. Younger children under two are increasingly affected. In 2021, Kajiado had visceral leishmaniasis prompting surveys by KEMRI and ICIPE; authorities aim to establish treatment centers and strengthen disease management.

articleHeadline: Detectan virus marino que habría infectado a humanos y provoca pérdida de visión
articleSummary: Covert Mortality Nodavirus (CMNV), a marine nodavirus previously studied in aquaculture, has been linked to human infections in China, suggesting possible zoonotic spillover. First identified in 2014, CMNV devastates aquaculture species, causing up to 80% mortality in shrimp and damaging nervous, muscular, and ocular tissues. Reported human cases in China are characterized by vision loss, with all cases sharing exposure to raw seafood or seafood-handling environments. There is currently no evidence of human-to-human transmission. CMNV's ability to infect multiple species and persist in diverse aquatic settings underscores potential spillover risk from marine ecosystems. The finding, published in Nature Microbiology (2026), prompts intensified surveillance of marine-origin pathogens and reinforces basic preventive measures for those handling seafood to mitigate exposure while research continues.
notes: CMNV（Covert Mortality Nodavirus）は養殖産業で既知の海洋ウイルスだが、ヒト感染が新たに報告された。Nature Microbiology（2026年）に発表されたため、国際的な学術的関心が高い。視力喪失などの臨床症状の報告あり。ヒト-ヒト感染の証拠なし。食品安全との関連性あり（生シーフード・処理環境での暴露）。動物およぐ環境への影響も記載されている。

articleHeadline: El comercio de especies aumenta la transmisión de patógenos y el riesgo de pandemias
articleSummary: Wildlife trade, legal or illegal, markedly increases pathogen transmission between animals and humans, raising epidemic and pandemic risk and calling for tighter biosurveillance to limit contact with virus- or parasite-carrying wildlife. A Lausanne University study (Ecology and Evolution) quantified this link, published in Science. By integrating four decades of wildlife import/export data with host–pathogen networks, researchers found traded wild mammals are 1.5x more likely to transmit pathogens to humans than non-traded species, with higher risk when trade is illegal or animals are kept as live pets. Each decade in markets adds about one extra shared pathogen. The analysis covers wild mammals, including wild-caught and captive-bred individuals and derivatives (skins, horns) and exotic pets. Transmission risk starts with hunting, skinning, and transport; historical examples include 2003 monkeypox in the United States and COVID-19 linked to Wuhan markets. Calls for stronger biosurveillance; CITES centers on extinction, not transmission. As of 9 April 2026.
notes: 記事はスイス・ローザンヌ大学による学術研究に基づいた分析であり、野生動物取引と病原体伝播のリスク関連性を定量化している。2003年の米国サル痘とCOVID-19武漢市場関連の具体例が言及されている。ただし、現在進行中の具体的な感染症発生イベントの報告ではなく、構造的リスク警告が主体。Mpox、Mpox Clade I/II、COVID-19が複数疾患として登録されているが、記事本体では具体的な現在の流行状況ではなく、取引との関連性の一般的考察と歴史的事例が中心。続報の監視が必要。

articleSummary: Hidden-Mortality Nodavirus is linked to a surge of ocular diseases in China, with epidemiological data showing 71.4% of investigated cases reporting direct exposure to aquatic animals such as seafood and fish. articleHeadline: Cholera Evolution and Bacterial Defense Mechanisms - News Directory 3
articleSummary: Cholera (Vibrio cholerae) seventh pandemic El Tor lineage shows that Bangladesh strains with loss of phage-defense genes have higher risk of severe disease and greater transmission beyond Bangladesh. A long-term genomic study reports rapid changes in phage-defense genes and mobile elements driven by an ongoing arms race with bacteriophages ICP1, ICP2, and ICP3 isolated from patient stools. ICP1 has evolved a CRISPR-Cas countermeasure against bacterial defense islands; V. cholerae may acquire new defenses via DNA uptake. A 2018 Bangladesh lineage replacement coincided with rapid anti-defense evolution in ICP1. Transmission between India and Bangladesh occurs, yet lineages appear largely separated by national borders over 20 years. The Ganges Basin, not the Ganges Delta, is identified as the probable global pandemic launch pad. Findings, published in Nature on 1 April 2026, reshape understanding of cholera evolution and cross-border spread.

articleSummary: Nipah virus, a bat-borne zoonosis with fruit bats as the natural reservoir, is the focus. Thailand has not reported human Nipah cases, but ecological studies show bat exposure evidence (antibodies and viral genetic material) in several provinces, signaling ongoing risk. Historically, Nipah outbreaks have occurred since the 1990s in Malaysia, Singapore, Bangladesh, India, and the Philippines, including West Bengal, India. Nipah infection typically presents with fever, headache, or pneumonia and can rapidly progress to acute encephalitis, with high case fatality. Transmission occurs animal-to-human and human-to-human, notably within households and hospitals. The WHO lists Nipah as a priority pathogen for vaccine development and therapeutics. Unlike COVID-19, Nipah outbreaks are cluster-based and highly lethal, with sector-specific economic impacts. For Thailand’s insurance sector, Nipah represents a strategic risk requiring scenario testing, risk frameworks, and One Health approaches to product design and risk communication.

articleSummary: Roche Diagnostics Korea introduces cobas Malaria PCR testing at Hanmaeum Blood Center, the nation’s first implementation of malaria nucleic acid testing (NAT) on all donated blood. The Asia-Pacific region’s first full-volume malaria NAT screening on blood donations uses the cobas Malaria assay on automated cobas 5800/6800/8800 systems, complementing existing immunoassays with DNA-based detection of low parasite levels. This advance aims to strengthen transfusion safety and rationalize post-exposure blood donation deferrals. WHO’s 2022 data show 247 million malaria cases globally in 2021 across 84 countries. Korea has treated malaria elimination as a WHO priority since 2017; previously, at-risk travelers faced a one-year deferral, far above the WHO four-month guideline, excluding roughly 30,000 potential donors annually. Experts expect the PCR-based approach to shorten deferral periods, stabilize blood supply, and enhance patient safety, with statements from Hanmaeum Blood Center officials and Roche Korea.

articleSummary: First detection of South Africa Type I foot-and-mouth disease virus (FMDV) in China, with confirmed outbreaks in Xinjiang Yining County and Gansu Gulang County (Wuwei City). Live pig movement is banned; Ningxia Pengyang and surrounding live livestock markets have closed. Two targeted vaccines received emergency approvals on Apr 1 and Apr 6 from Zhongnongweit and Bio-Stock Co., respectively: one subunit vaccine and one inactivated vaccine. The novel FMDV is a positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus, less stable than African swine fever virus, mainly affecting cattle and sheep; infections in pigs are rare. Adult cattle show mild symptoms; calf mortality reportedly 50–90%. No human deaths or significant human infection reported. Domestic cattle and sheep herds total about 100 million and 280 million, respectively, with Xinjiang, Gansu, and Ningxia accounting for roughly 16% of national cattle. The outbreak may drive herd culling and lift beef prices, while hog farming remains less affected but boosts investment sentiment.

articleSummary: Cat bites are not minor: CDC notes 20–80% of cat bites or scratches become infected. The primary offender is Pasteurella multocida, present in 70–90% of cats and found in about 75% of bite wounds. Infections usually appear within 24–48 hours with pain, swelling, redness, and inflammation, and may progress to cellulitis or abscess; sepsis is rare. Bites can also transmit other diseases, including cat scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) with fever and lymphadenopathy 1–3 weeks after exposure; rabies risk remains, especially from wild cats; tetanus risk; and, rarely, sporotrichosis. Initial care: wash the wound with running water and soap for at least 5 minutes, do not seal the wound, and seek medical care promptly. Seek medical attention if the wound is deep, hard to clean, red, swollen, painful, feverish, rabies status unknown, or tetanus vaccine >5 years old. Antibiotics can treat most cases.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Chikungunya in Tucumán: cases rise by 60% and door-to-door checks are strengthened.
articleHeadline: Chikungunya en Tucumán: los casos suben un 60% y refuerzan controles casa por casa
articleSummary: Chikungunya in Tucumán, Argentina: cases rise 60% to 93 in the province, concentrated in the southeast sector of San Miguel de Tucumán and El Manantial. All infections were detected through active house-to-house surveillance; no hospitalizations and more than half have recovered. The week-over-week increase is from 36 to 93. Aedes aegypti mosquitoes breed in water-filled containers, with recent rains exacerbating risk. Authorities have reinforced door-to-door checks, enabling immediate home interventions, elimination of breeding sites, and targeted fumigation in affected areas. The outbreak reflects regional transmission pressures; neighboring Bolivia, Brazil, Paraguay, and Argentina’s Salta report cases. Symptoms include high fever, intense joint pain, body aches, and sometimes rash days after fever onset. Preventive guidance emphasizes repellents, eliminating water-collecting objects, and seeking medical care promptly. No severe cases or hospitalizations reported; response focuses on containment through active surveillance.

articleHeadlineTranslated: Chickenpox in Adults Is Prone to Secondary Infection, Pneumonia, and Encephalitis.
articleHeadline: Thủy đậu ở người lớn dễ bội nhiễm, viêm phổi, viêm não
articleSummary: Varicella (chickenpox) in adults at Cam Khe Regional Medical Center, Phu Tho Province, Vietnam, has progressed to severe secondary bacterial infection, with several cases reported. A 35-year-old patient from Phu Khe commune presented with high fever, rigors, and scattered vesicular skin lesions; on admission his condition worsened with nodules and pustulation, accompanied by intense pruritus. Clinicians diagnosed varicella with secondary infection, a complication that can arise when skin lesions are not properly cared for or scratched. He received aggressive management: infection control, antipyretics, fluid and electrolyte replacement, and local wound care. After two days, fever diminished, vesicles crusted, itching eased, and overall status stabilized. Dr. Nguyen Van Phong emphasizes varicella is typically mild but can cause dangerous outcomes such as secondary skin infection, pneumonia, and rare encephalitis. Advice: seek prompt medical evaluation, avoid scratching or rupturing lesions, maintain skin hygiene, isolate to prevent transmission, and vaccination remains a preventive measure.
